title: What artificial intelligence includes
summary: A rigorous map of artificial intelligence as a chain from objectives and data through learning, inference, decisions, operations, and social consequence.
sources: ACM: Alan Turing and machine intelligence
html:
Artificial intelligence is easier to understand when it is treated as a system design discipline rather than a catalogue of model names. The field combines representations, rules, search, probability, optimization, learned functions, software infrastructure, human decisions, and institutions. A model supplies one transformation inside that system. The rest of the chain decides what the transformation means, what evidence supports it, and what authority its output receives.

When fixed rules stop being enough

Ordinary software works well when a designer can enumerate the relevant states and write the correct response. AI becomes useful when the environment is too variable, the desired mapping is too hard to specify directly, or the system must improve from experience. That motivation does not make a learned model the default for every task.

  • Perception compresses a variable world. A camera image, waveform, or document contains far more raw detail than a downstream decision needs. Perception systems map that signal into useful objects, events, text, locations, or embeddings. Their output remains an estimate shaped by sensors, labels, and context; it is not direct access to reality.
  • Prediction estimates an unknown quantity. A classifier estimates a category, a regressor estimates a number, and a ranking model orders candidates. The useful object is often a conditional distribution or score. The product still needs a threshold, cost model, and fallback before that estimate becomes a decision.
  • Search and planning choose among possibilities. Game playing, routing, scheduling, theorem proving, and constraint satisfaction can require intelligence without fitting a neural network. An algorithm explores states under rules and an objective. Learned heuristics can guide the search, but the state representation and legal actions still define the problem.
  • Generation models a space of possible outputs. Text, image, audio, video, code, and molecular generators produce candidates from a learned distribution. Fluency measures how plausible an output is under that distribution. It does not establish factual accuracy, legal validity, executability, or suitability for a particular user.
  • Control closes the loop. A controller observes a changing environment, chooses an action, receives a new observation, and repeats. Latency, stability, actuator limits, partial observability, and recovery become part of correctness because prediction errors now alter the next state.
THE GOTCHA

“This task uses judgment” is not enough to justify machine learning. If a rule, query, calculator, or solver can own the requirement with explicit guarantees, adding a probabilistic model increases uncertainty without adding necessary capability.

AI systems, models, and adjacent terms

A precise vocabulary prevents category errors. These terms describe different layers or methods. They overlap, but none can be used as a synonym for all the others.

  • An AI system produces outputs that influence an environment. A useful operational definition includes objectives, inputs, computation, outputs, autonomy, people, and context of use. NIST treats AI as a machine-based system that produces predictions, recommendations, or decisions for real or virtual environments. The system boundary therefore extends beyond model weights.
  • Machine learning fits behavior from data. The developer chooses a representation, model family, objective, optimization process, and evaluation design. Training data changes parameters so the model performs a task on examples it did not memorize exactly. Generalization to a target population is the central claim and must be measured.
  • Deep learning uses layered differentiable models. Layers compose linear transformations, nonlinearities, normalization, routing, and memory. Depth lets the system build intermediate representations. It does not remove the need to define data, objectives, numerical precision, evaluation, or the action taken from the output.
  • A foundation model is trained for broad adaptation. Large-scale pretraining creates a reusable representation that can support prompting, retrieval, fine-tuning, tool use, or task-specific heads. “Foundation” describes its role in an ecosystem of downstream systems. It does not mean the model is complete, universal, or authoritative.
  • Generative AI produces structured candidates. Autoregressive models predict the next unit; diffusion models reverse a corruption process; other families model data in different ways. The application must distinguish sampling from verification. A generated SQL query, diagnosis, citation, or plan becomes trustworthy only after the relevant external check.
  • An agent couples a policy to an environment. The agent receives observations, maintains state, chooses actions, invokes tools, and reacts to results. The language model may propose the next action, while the harness owns permissions, budgets, retries, durable state, and stopping conditions. Agency is a system property, not a personality assigned to a chatbot.
THE GOTCHA

A capable model can sit inside an incapable system, and a reliable system can use a modest model. Model benchmarks compare learned components under a protocol; product claims require evidence about the complete operating path.

From symbolic programs to foundation models

AI did not progress through one clean replacement sequence. Symbolic reasoning, probabilistic modeling, control, search, neural networks, and human-computer interaction developed in parallel. Each wave solved a different bottleneck and exposed a different failure mode.

  • 1950 — Alan Turing. “Computing Machinery and Intelligence” shifted an abstract debate about thought toward observable performance and described learning machines as a plausible route. The lasting contribution was methodological: specify a testable interaction rather than arguing from an undefined essence.
  • 1956 — the Dartmouth research project. The proposal named artificial intelligence and framed learning, abstraction, language, problem solving, and self-improvement as parts of one program. Early optimism underestimated how representation, compute, data, and open-world knowledge constrain each part.
  • 1960s–1980s — symbols, search, and expert systems. Programs manipulated formal states, rules, and knowledge bases. They achieved strong results in bounded domains because their representations were explicit. Knowledge acquisition, exception handling, and maintenance became the bottlenecks as domains grew.
  • 1990s–2000s — statistical learning. More data, probabilistic methods, kernels, ensembles, and standardized benchmarks shifted emphasis from encoding every rule to estimating behavior from samples. This made generalization measurable while introducing dependence on dataset construction and train-test assumptions.
  • 2012 — deep learning at computer-vision scale. AlexNet combined a large labeled dataset, GPU computation, convolutional networks, and practical training techniques. The event matters as a systems result: architecture alone did not cause the jump, and later progress continued to depend on hardware and data pipelines.
  • 2017 onward — attention, scale, and adaptation. Transformers enabled highly parallel training over sequences. Self-supervised objectives converted raw data into learning signals. Scaling and instruction tuning produced models that could adapt through context, while retrieval and tools reintroduced explicit external systems around the learned core.
1950Turing reframes machine intelligence as observable behavior and learning.
1956The Dartmouth proposal gives the field its name and an explicit research program.
1980sExpert systems scale encoded knowledge, then expose maintenance and brittleness costs.
1990s–2000sStatistical learning shifts attention toward data, generalization, and benchmarked prediction.
2012AlexNet demonstrates the combined effect of data, GPUs, neural networks, and training practice.
2017Transformers make attention-centered sequence modeling highly parallel during training.
2020sFoundation models turn one pretrained representation into a platform for many adapted tasks.
THE GOTCHA

Historical narratives often credit one algorithm while hiding the enabling dataset, hardware, benchmark, software stack, and labor. Treat every breakthrough as a coupled system and ask which constraint actually moved.

The building blocks and their dependency order

Every AI product can be read as a path from the world to an outcome and back again. The building blocks appear in dependency order below. Later blocks cannot repair information that an earlier block erased, and a technically correct early block cannot authorize a harmful later decision.

  • Objectives define what “better” means. A business wish becomes a measurable target, loss, reward, or constraint. The objective needs a population, time horizon, error costs, and owner. Proxy objectives are unavoidable in many domains, so teams must state what the proxy omits and how gaming would appear.
  • Data records a process, not the world itself. Examples come from sensors, transactions, users, policies, annotators, and prior systems. Sampling decides who appears. Labels encode definitions and delays. Splits approximate a future deployment condition. Provenance is therefore part of the model specification.
  • Representation determines what computation can see. A tokenizer segments text, a feature pipeline maps records, and an encoder maps media into tensors. Shape, units, coordinate frames, missing-value conventions, and authorization must survive this boundary. An omitted distinction cannot be recovered reliably downstream.
  • Computation maps representations to candidates. Rules, search procedures, optimizers, probabilistic models, neural networks, retrieval indexes, and simulators each provide different guarantees. Hybrid systems work when each component owns the claim it can actually verify.
  • Decision policy converts scores into actions. A probability becomes an alert only after a threshold. A ranked list becomes a recommendation only after capacity and policy constraints. A generated action becomes executable only after schema validation and authorization. This layer assigns real consequence.
  • Feedback changes the next operating condition. User behavior, interventions, retraining data, model updates, and monitoring close the loop. The deployed policy selects which outcomes become visible. Without careful experiment design, apparent improvement can be feedback bias rather than better performance.
THE GOTCHA

End-to-end success cannot be inferred from component tests. The composed system must preserve identity, units, ordering, evidence, and authority across every transition.

Data and representation define the observable world

A learning system never receives reality directly. It receives measurements selected by a collection process and encoded into a representation. This boundary decides which people, events, distinctions, and time relationships the model can use. Data quality therefore means fitness for a stated decision, not merely a clean table.

  • The unit of observation anchors every row. A row may describe a person, account, session, device, image, token, event, or time window. Mixing these units creates false sample counts and leakage. Repeated observations from one person are correlated; frames from one video share a scene; events after an outcome cannot predict that outcome at decision time.
  • Sampling determines the population represented. Convenience data reflects who used an existing product, passed a prior filter, granted consent, remained measurable, or received a label. A large sample reduces random error around that selected population. It does not repair systematic exclusion or make the sample representative of a different deployment population.
  • Labels encode an operational definition. “Fraud,” “toxicity,” “quality,” and “success” are not raw facts waiting in storage. They depend on policy, observation windows, annotator instructions, adjudication, and delayed outcomes. Record who produced each label, what evidence they saw, how disagreement was handled, and when the label became available.
  • Features and tokens preserve some distinctions and erase others. A feature pipeline chooses units, normalization, category vocabularies, missing-value semantics, and aggregation windows. A tokenizer chooses text segments and vocabulary coverage. Image and audio preprocessing choose resolution, sampling, cropping, and dynamic range. Each choice creates invariances and blind spots before the model runs.
  • Embeddings create task-shaped geometry. An encoder maps items to vectors so downstream computations can compare or transform them. Nearness reflects the objective and examples used to train that encoder. Similar vectors may indicate topical, stylistic, behavioral, or visual similarity; they do not automatically establish identity, truth, fairness, or causal relationship.
  • Provenance and authorization travel with the record. Source, collection time, consent or license, transformation version, retention rule, and access scope determine whether a record may be used. Copying content into a training set or vector index does not erase these obligations. Derived artifacts need deletion and access paths connected to their sources.
  • Splits simulate the future boundary. Random splits work only when future observations are exchangeable with the sample and related records cannot cross partitions. Time, geography, customer, document family, device, and policy regime often require grouped or temporal splits. Fit scalers, vocabularies, imputers, and feature selectors after this boundary exists.
THE GOTCHA

A dataset can have no missing cells and still be unusable because it measures the wrong population, leaks future information, embeds an obsolete policy, or lacks permission for the intended use. Schema validity proves structure; provenance and evaluation establish meaning.

Learning is an optimization claim and a generalization claim

Training changes parameters to reduce an objective on observed data. That mechanical fact is weaker than the product claim: that the resulting behavior will remain useful on future cases drawn from the intended operating population.

  • Supervised learning uses explicit targets. Examples pair inputs with labels or numerical outcomes. Classification loss teaches relative probabilities; regression loss penalizes numerical error. Label timing and availability matter because a feature that exists after the decision creates leakage even when the code is correct.
  • Self-supervision manufactures targets from raw structure. A language model predicts hidden or subsequent tokens; a vision model may reconstruct masked patches or align views. This unlocks large unlabeled corpora, but the pretraining objective rewards statistical prediction rather than every downstream property users value.
  • Unsupervised methods expose structure relative to a chosen geometry. Clustering, dimensionality reduction, density estimation, and anomaly detection work without task labels, but they still depend on features, scaling, distance, neighborhood, and capacity choices. A visible cluster is a hypothesis about the representation. It becomes useful only after stability checks and external evidence connect it to the real domain.
  • Reinforcement learning uses consequences over trajectories. An agent receives reward after actions in an environment. Credit assignment estimates which earlier actions contributed to later outcomes. The policy changes the data it encounters, so off-policy evidence and reward misspecification create failure modes absent from static supervised datasets.
  • Optimization finds parameters under numerical constraints. Gradient-based training follows local derivatives through a computation graph. Learning rate, batch construction, precision, initialization, regularization, and optimizer state shape the path. A decreasing training loss proves only that this combined procedure fits its own objective.
  • Generalization requires a protected comparison. A held-out set estimates behavior under the population encoded by its sampling and split rule. Temporal, geographic, user-level, adversarial, and policy shifts need corresponding evaluations. Repeatedly selecting against the same test set turns it into training data for the research process.
  • Adaptation trades specialization against retained capability. Fine-tuning updates weights on task or preference data; parameter-efficient methods constrain which updates are learned; distillation transfers behavior into another model; prompting and retrieval adapt behavior without ordinary weight updates. Every route changes a different artifact and creates different costs for versioning, forgetting, latency, privacy, and rollback.
THE GOTCHA

More training compute can optimize the wrong objective more efficiently. Diagnose the target, data path, split, and metric before treating scale as the missing ingredient.

Inference is a composed runtime, not one model call

At inference time, a trained model receives new inputs and produces outputs without the ordinary weight updates of training. Modern applications surround that pass with retrieval, caches, tools, validators, routing, and human review. These components determine both capability and failure behavior.

  • Prompting changes context. Instructions, examples, conversation history, and retrieved passages condition a particular request. They consume a finite context budget and can conflict. Prompting does not teach durable knowledge to the weights, and text inside the prompt remains untrusted input when it comes from users or documents.
  • Retrieval brings external evidence into scope. Lexical and vector indexes generate candidates; rerankers order them; authorization filters them; citations connect output claims to sources. Retrieval recall places a ceiling on grounded generation because a model cannot reliably cite evidence the system never supplied.
  • Tools provide authoritative operations. A calculator owns arithmetic, a database owns records, a compiler owns syntax and execution checks, and an API owns an external action. The model proposes structured calls. Deterministic code validates arguments, checks permission, executes, records effects, and returns typed results.
  • Memory has several incompatible meanings. A context window holds request-local tokens. A cache reuses computation. A vector store retrieves prior artifacts. A database preserves durable state. Fine-tuning changes weights. Calling all five “memory” hides retention, deletion, consistency, and privacy boundaries.
  • Serving adds queues and shared capacity. Tokenization, network transfer, prefill, autoregressive decode, batching, KV-cache allocation, and tool latency contribute to response time. Throughput and tail latency trade against each other. The model can be fast in isolation while the application misses its service objective.
WORKED SYSTEM

Answering “Why is my invoice higher?”

  1. Identify the customer and authorize access. Authentication and access control own identity. A language model must never infer or override this boundary.
  2. Fetch the current invoice. A database query retrieves the authoritative amount, line items, currency, and billing period. Retrieval success is measured separately from answer quality.
  3. Recompute deterministic totals. A calculator checks quantities, rates, taxes, discounts, and rounding. Arithmetic stays outside free-form generation.
  4. Retrieve applicable policy. The system searches versioned contract and pricing documents effective for that billing period. Every explanation claim must point to retrieved evidence.
  5. Generate the explanation. A language model converts structured facts into clear prose under an output schema. It may explain; it may not change the invoice or invent a missing reason.
  6. Validate and route. Code checks totals, citations, currency, and unsupported claims. A dispute or missing record routes to a human with the same evidence bundle.

Acceptance test. On a fixed set of invoices, every amount must match deterministic recomputation, every policy claim must cite the effective document, unauthorized records must remain inaccessible, and unsupported cases must abstain.

THE GOTCHA

A successful answer does not reveal which subsystem caused it. Preserve traces that identify the prompt version, retrieved evidence, model version, tool calls, validation result, latency, and user-visible outcome.

Evaluation must match the decision

A metric is a compressed answer to a specific question. Accuracy, loss, win rate, pass rate, latency, cost, calibration, and safety tests describe different properties. Selecting a convenient number before defining the decision creates precise evidence for the wrong claim.

  • Start with the unit of analysis. Decide whether one example represents a user, message, session, patient, device, document, or event. Related records must remain grouped when leakage across the split would make the test easier than deployment. State the target population and sampling period.
  • Use a baseline that exposes added value. Compare against a rule, lookup, simple statistical model, prior release, or human workflow. A complex model that beats no credible baseline has not justified its extra cost, opacity, or operational surface. Baselines also reveal when the task is mostly solved by prevalence.
  • Measure the operating point. A classifier needs a threshold; a retrieval system needs k; a generator needs decoding settings; an agent needs budgets and stopping conditions. Report the configuration alongside the score because a metric without its operating point cannot predict product behavior.
  • Inspect uncertainty and slices. Aggregate values hide sample variation and concentrated harm. Report confidence intervals or repeated-run variation where applicable. Slice by conditions likely to change performance, but keep enough samples and avoid turning exploratory slices into unsupported causal stories.
  • Test the complete path. Component evaluations isolate causes; end-to-end evaluations capture composition. A production release needs both. Include malformed inputs, missing evidence, dependency failure, permission denial, cancellation, overload, and abstention rather than measuring only ordinary success cases.
  • Separate demonstration, benchmark, and field evidence. A demonstration establishes possibility under one setup. A benchmark compares systems under a protocol. A controlled experiment estimates causal effect. Field monitoring observes behavior under real incentives and changing conditions. Each supports a different claim.
THE GOTCHA

A higher average score can make the product worse when it changes calibration, latency, cost, subgroup error, or the cases sent to human review. Choose metrics from the decision and its failure costs, then freeze the evaluation protocol before comparing models.

Choose the smallest sufficient system

Architecture begins by decomposing the job into claims and assigning each claim to the component with the right guarantee. This keeps learned approximation where it adds value and preserves deterministic ownership for identity, arithmetic, policy, evidence, and irreversible effects.

  • Write the decision before the model. State the user, input available at decision time, output contract, action, latency budget, acceptable abstention, and harm from false positive and false negative errors. If these are unknown, model selection is premature.
  • Separate facts from transformations. Identify authoritative records, computations that must be exact, evidence that must be retrieved, predictions that require uncertainty, and prose that can be generated. Give each boundary a typed input and output plus an owner.
  • Add autonomy only with control. A one-shot suggestion, a reviewed draft, a bounded tool call, and an autonomous multi-step workflow have different blast radii. Increasing autonomy requires stronger permissions, budgets, sandboxing, observability, cancellation, and recovery.
  • Price the accepted outcome. Count model inference, retrieval, storage, networking, retries, review, idle capacity, and incidents. Compare alternatives at equal quality and reliability. A cheaper token can produce a more expensive completed task when it increases correction or failure.
  • Version the whole release. Weights, tokenizer, prompt, preprocessing, feature definitions, retrieval index, tool policy, runtime, and evaluation set form one compatible artifact set. Canary and rollback procedures must exercise that same composition.

THE GOTCHA

Starting with a general model encourages every downstream requirement to become prompt text. Prompt text cannot enforce database consistency, access control, numerical correctness, transactionality, or physical safety.

Operations, feedback, and governance keep the claim true

Deployment changes the problem from fitting a model to maintaining a socio-technical service. Users adapt, source systems change, dependencies fail, costs move, and model outputs influence future data. Reliability requires ownership and evidence throughout that lifecycle.

  • Version the release as a compatible set. Weights alone do not identify behavior. Record the tokenizer, feature pipeline, prompt and templates, retrieval corpus and embedding model, tool schemas and policies, runtime libraries, numerical precision, decoding settings, and evaluation suite. A rollback must restore a compatible combination rather than one familiar file.
  • Canaries test semantics as well as availability. A health endpoint proves that a process responds. A useful canary sends representative requests through authentication, retrieval, inference, validation, and side-effect controls. It compares output quality, evidence support, latency, cost, and refusal behavior with the current release before traffic expands.
  • Monitoring follows the user-visible causal path. Separate queue time, preprocessing, retrieval, model prefill, decoding, tool calls, validation, and commit time. Track input and outcome distributions, abstention, override, complaint, and incident rates. Aggregate infrastructure telemetry cannot reveal a concentrated semantic failure without task-level signals.
  • Feedback is selected by the deployed policy. A recommendation changes clicks; a moderation model changes visible content; an approval model changes who receives an outcome. Later labels therefore describe a world partly created by the model. Randomized exploration, shadow evaluation, audits, and causal methods may be needed to distinguish improvement from self-confirmation.
  • Incident response requires retained evidence and bounded authority. Teams need to reconstruct which version, context, sources, tools, permissions, and decisions produced an effect. Logs must retain enough structure for diagnosis while minimizing sensitive content. Rate limits, transaction boundaries, approval gates, and kill switches limit damage before diagnosis finishes.
  • Governance assigns decisions to named actors. Model developers, application teams, data owners, domain experts, operators, risk functions, users, and affected communities see different failure modes. Governance defines who accepts a use, who can halt it, who reviews changes, who receives incident reports, and how an affected person obtains explanation or recourse.
  • Retirement is an engineering state. A model may become unsafe, uneconomic, unsupported, legally incompatible, or simply worse than its replacement. Retirement includes traffic migration, dependent-system discovery, archive or deletion of data and indexes, revocation of credentials, reproducibility requirements, and a clear end to monitoring obligations.
THE GOTCHA

A stable dashboard can hide a changing system when the monitored metric is downstream of the model’s own selection policy. Preserve external reference samples and field outcomes that the model cannot improve merely by changing what becomes visible.

Read every AI claim as a stack of contracts

The field becomes coherent when every layer is asked to make only the claim its evidence supports. Hardware executes numerical operations. Learning fits a representation under an objective. Evaluation estimates behavior under a protocol. Applications bind that behavior to evidence and tools. Organizations assign responsibility. Institutions decide which uses are legitimate.

  • Representation contract. What does each input mean, which distinctions were preserved, where did it come from, and what uncertainty or missingness does it carry?
  • Learning contract. Which objective changed which parameters using which data, and why should that procedure capture structure that transfers beyond the sample?
  • Behavior contract. Which population, tasks, baselines, metrics, slices, and failure tests support the claimed capability?
  • System contract. Which retrieval, tools, memory, permissions, validators, people, and service dependencies compose the observed result?
  • Operational contract. Who owns monitoring, incident response, update compatibility, rollback, retention, cost, and retirement?
  • Legitimacy contract. Who benefits, who absorbs errors, what authority does the system receive, and how can an affected person challenge or escape the decision?
  • Dependency contract. Which hardware, energy, networks, vendors, labor, licenses, and supply chains keep the system available, and what happens when one of them changes or disappears?
  • Change contract. Which evidence must be rerun after a new model, prompt, dataset, policy, tool, or user population enters the system, and who decides whether the earlier claim still holds?
THE GOTCHA

No lower layer can certify the one above it. Correct floating-point arithmetic does not prove a useful model; a useful model does not prove a reliable product; a reliable product does not prove a legitimate use.
